title: Microsoft Teams: report suspicious guest invitations to your admin
notes: claim 59: severity major on a rationale: risk rating lowered to minor; ratings are judgements and cannot hold a page
claim 60: severity major on a rationale: risk rating lowered to minor; ratings are judgements and cannot hold a page
summary: Hold: the briefing says Microsoft has not documented the role needed to configure reporting, but its cited Defender page explicitly names Teams Administrator or Global Administrator. The rollout, reporting paths and command are supported; the risk rationale also needs to distinguish undocumented access and automatic-action effects from guarantees that none exist.

claims.where: title; summary; What's changing; Why it matters
claims.claim: Teams will enable users to report suspicious guest invitations directly to their IT admin for review.
claims.quote: Microsoft Teams will enable users to report suspicious guest invitations directly from Teams. When users receive an unexpected or potentially malicious guest invitation, they can report it to their IT admin for review

claims.where: What's changing; Why it matters; Scope
claims.claim: These invitations ask users to join another organisation as a guest and can be used for phishing or other abuse.
claims.quote: When users receive an unexpected or potentially malicious invitation to join another organization as a guest, they can report it to their IT admin for review, helping identify and mitigate phishing and other abuse through guest invitations.

claims.claim: The cited pages do not state the Teams admin center role needed to edit the reporting messaging-policy setting.
claims.quote: To view or configure user reporting in the Teams admin center, you need to be a member of the Global Administrator* or Teams Administrator roles.
claims.fix: Replace the configuration-role absence with: 'To configure user reporting in the Teams admin center, Microsoft names Teams Administrator or Global Administrator; use the least-privileged suitable role.' Cite https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-office-365/submissions-teams#user-reporting-settings-for-teams-items. Do not extend these configuration roles to report access without evidence.

claims.claim: The cited pages do not state a role specifically required to view the User reported security submissions report.
claims.quote: Searched: "User reported security submissions" "role". Read end-user-reported-security-signal and submissions-teams; the former states no access role, while the latter's Teams Administrator/Global Administrator requirement concerns viewing or configuring reporting settings, not this report.

claims.claim: Guest-invitation reporting adds no new access.
claims.quote: Searched: "Teams" "guest invitations" reporting permissions access autonomous. Read the roadmap, MC1530615 and the cited reporting pages; none explicitly establishes that this feature adds no access. The notice confirms report sharing, not an access-boundary guarantee.
claims.fix: Remove 'adds no new access' from the risk rationale. Ground the judgement in the verified facts instead: 'Low. Reporting is user-initiated, and the notice places it under the existing Report a security concern messaging-policy setting; reports are shared with admins and Microsoft.'

claims.claim: Guest-invitation reporting adds no autonomous action.
claims.quote: Searched: "Teams" "guest invitation" report notification automatic remediation; "Teams" "guest invitations" reporting permissions access autonomous. Read MC1530615 and the reporting pages; they do not establish that automatic post-report actions cannot occur.
claims.fix: Replace the categorical 'adds no ... autonomous action' with 'the notice describes no autonomous action', matching the qualified wording in Risk assessment and retaining the open question about automatic remediation.
